content: Client-managed groups have been implemented to support adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) in various contexts, including family groups, key populations, and unstable settings. These groups aim to enhance treatment outcomes by fostering a sense of community and shared responsibility among participants. Facility-based individual models, often referred to as fast-track or quick pick-up, extend beyond simply increasing the duration of ART refills. These models designate specific locations, such as pharmacies, and times for ART refills, eliminating the need for consultations with healthcare workers for clinical reviews or prescriptions. This approach significantly reduces the time patients spend at clinics. Evidence from these models has shown reduced waiting times, fewer missed appointments, and lower costs from both societal and health ministry perspectives. Additionally, these models have demonstrated positive impacts on patient retention and viral load suppression, even in low-prevalence and politically unstable settings, as well as for children. A study involving over 22,000 children across six sub-Saharan African countries found that 66% of children had their ART refills extended beyond one month. Over a five-year period, viral load suppression rates remained high, ranging from 79% to 85%. However, 6% of children were lost to follow-up, and 2% died. Community-based individual models vary based on the location and provider of services. These include fixed community points (such as private or community pharmacies), mobile outreach ART delivery, and home delivery. High retention rates have been reported in countries like the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Africa, Uganda, and Zambia. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, ART refills are provided at community sites managed by treatment-literate peers. Fixed community ART delivery points have also been used to provide six-month ART refills and have been implemented for children and key populations through drop-in centers. Home delivery of ART has been studied in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda, with mixed results regarding retention and mortality. In settings where costs were analyzed, home delivery was found to be less expensive for both health services and patients compared to facility-based care. However, the feasibility and relevance of home delivery depend on factors such as health system capacity, distance, and stigma. Mobile outreach approaches, while less studied, have the potential to integrate the delivery of other health services at the community level. A recent systematic review of differentiated service delivery models for HIV treatment included 29 publications describing 37 models. Among these, 19% were facility-based individual models, 32% were individual models based outside facilities, 14% were client-led groups, and 35% were healthcare worker-led groups. Retention rates in most differentiated service delivery models were within 5 percentage points of those for conventional care, and when no comparison was provided, retention generally exceeded 80%. People-centered care is a critical component of effective HIV programs. This approach focuses on organizing care around the health needs, preferences, and expectations of individuals and communities while upholding dignity and respect, particularly for vulnerable populations. It also emphasizes engaging and supporting individuals and families to actively participate in their care through informed decision-making. Safe, acceptable, and timely clinical and non-clinical services should be provided to reduce HIV-related morbidity and mortality, improve health outcomes, and enhance quality of life. Efficient and effective use of resources is also a priority. Interventions to improve relationships between patients and healthcare providers include providing friendly and welcoming services, conducting sensitization training for healthcare providers to address stigma and discrimination, offering individualized adherence counseling, facilitating client education, and providing feedback to healthcare workers on patient concerns and service quality. These approaches have shown beneficial effects across the HIV care cascade, including improved ART uptake, adherence, and viral load suppression. WHO recommends addressing stigma and discrimination in healthcare settings as a key strategy to ensure access to HIV care. Negative attitudes from healthcare workers contribute to loss of care and poor program outcomes, particularly for key populations who face structural barriers such as stigma, discrimination, and violence. Training healthcare providers to improve relationships with patients and support vulnerable groups is essential. ART initiation outside health facilities is recommended as an additional option to routine facility-based initiation. Community-based HIV testing and ART initiation can reduce delays in starting treatment, especially for individuals who face barriers to accessing health facilities. However, ensuring baseline assessments, counseling, and linkage to long-term care is crucial. Studies have shown that community ART initiation can increase treatment access and retention, particularly for vulnerable populations such as female sex workers. However, evidence for adolescents remains limited, and acceptability is uncertain. Implementation of community ART initiation requires adequate drug supply, laboratory services, trained health personnel, and referral mechanisms for higher-level care. A phased approach may be necessary, starting in settings with established community prevention and testing activities. National initiatives should include community HIV care to ensure quality of care. Research gaps include understanding client preferences for ART initiation and linkage to care by age, population, and setting. Further studies are needed to optimize community-based ART delivery and address the unique needs of different populations.
